criteria.name: Main idea
criteria.detail: Identifies the overall topic, purpose or message.
criteria.next: Practise identifying the topic and main message before focusing on detail.

criteria.name: Key detail
criteria.detail: Selects relevant names, facts, sequence or examples.
criteria.next: Use short listening texts to locate and record two key details.

criteria.name: Instructions
criteria.detail: Follows linked classroom directions and command words.
criteria.next: Rehearse multi-step instructions and curriculum command words with visuals.

criteria.name: Inference and viewpoint
criteria.detail: Recognises implied meaning, attitude or reason.
criteria.next: Model how tone, context and evidence reveal an unstated viewpoint.

criteria.name: Academic language
criteria.detail: Understands subject vocabulary, complex phrases and connective language.
criteria.next: Pre-teach high-utility academic words and connectives before listening tasks.

criteria.name: Participation and response
criteria.detail: Initiates, responds, clarifies and sustains interaction.
criteria.next: Build in rehearsed partner talk with prompts for asking and clarifying.

criteria.name: Fluency and intelligibility
criteria.detail: Communicates a connected message that listeners can follow.
criteria.next: Use short rehearsed explanations, then gradually reduce planning support.

criteria.name: Sentence control
criteria.detail: Uses an increasing range of accurate sentence patterns.
criteria.next: Model and practise one useful complex sentence pattern in curriculum talk.

criteria.name: Organisation
criteria.detail: Sequences ideas and uses cohesive language.
criteria.next: Provide oral frames for sequencing, comparing and explaining reasons.

criteria.name: Vocabulary and register
criteria.detail: Chooses precise social and academic language for audience and purpose.
criteria.next: Rehearse precise subject vocabulary and differences between informal and formal talk.

criteria.name: Gist and purpose
criteria.detail: Identifies topic, audience and purpose across text types.
criteria.next: Preview headings and visuals, then state the likely purpose before reading.

criteria.name: Retrieval and sequence
criteria.detail: Locates explicit information and follows relationships or sequence.
criteria.next: Practise scanning for evidence and ordering information from a short text.

criteria.name: Vocabulary in context
criteria.detail: Uses context, morphology and reference tools to work out meaning.
criteria.next: Teach how word parts and nearby sentences help infer an unfamiliar word.

criteria.name: Inference and evidence
criteria.detail: Combines clues and justifies an interpretation with text evidence.
criteria.next: Use evidence stems such as ‘This suggests… because the text says…’.

criteria.name: Text organisation
criteria.detail: Recognises cohesion, paragraph function and how information is organised.
criteria.next: Annotate paragraph purpose and the links created by pronouns and connectives.

criteria.name: Task and content
criteria.detail: Addresses the purpose with relevant, sufficiently developed ideas.
criteria.next: Plan content with audience, purpose and three relevant points before writing.

criteria.name: Organisation and cohesion
criteria.detail: Structures paragraphs and links ideas clearly.
criteria.next: Use a paragraph plan and practise a small range of accurate cohesive devices.

criteria.name: Vocabulary and register
criteria.detail: Selects precise language suited to the subject, audience and genre.
criteria.next: Build a reusable bank of subject vocabulary and formal alternatives.

criteria.name: Sentence range and control
criteria.detail: Uses varied sentence forms with control of grammar.
criteria.next: Combine short ideas using taught clauses and check verb agreement and tense.

criteria.name: Transcription
criteria.detail: Spelling and punctuation support clear meaning.
criteria.next: Edit one short section for high-frequency spelling and sentence punctuation.

community.name: Task set A — School community
community.listening: Read aloud at a natural pace: ‘The school council reviewed how pupils use the library after lessons. Most pupils valued the quiet tables, but several said that group discussion disturbed independent readers. The council proposed a bookable collaboration area near the entrance, with the silent zone kept at the back. Before any change, staff will trial the layout for four weeks and collect comments from pupils.’ Ask for the main proposal, two supporting details, the order of actions and one reason for the trial.
community.speaking: The pupil explains how a shared school space could meet different pupils’ needs. Ask one clarification question, one comparison question and one question requiring a justified recommendation.
community.reading: Use this original text: ‘A useful study space does more than provide desks. Pupils need to know what kind of work is expected in each area. Clear zones can reduce conflict: one area may support quiet concentration while another allows planned discussion. Yet a new layout alone will not solve every problem. Staff should observe how the space is used, invite feedback and adjust the plan. A successful change is therefore a process rather than a single decision.’ Ask about purpose, two explicit details, the meaning of “adjust”, an inference about observation, and the function of the final sentence.
community.writing: Write a recommendation to the school council about improving a study space. Explain the problem, propose a practical change, consider another viewpoint and justify a final recommendation. Suggested length: 120–180 words for KS3; 180–250 for KS4/Post-16.

technology.name: Task set B — Learning and technology
technology.listening: Read aloud at a natural pace: ‘Teachers noticed that some pupils could not complete online homework because they shared one device at home. The school plans to lend tablets for three nights at a time. Pupils will collect them from the learning centre and return them before registration on the fourth day. The first trial will involve two year groups so staff can check demand, damage and technical support.’ Ask for the problem, process, time detail, reason for a limited trial and likely staff concern.
technology.speaking: The pupil explains whether a device-lending scheme would improve learning. Prompt them to describe the process, weigh benefits and difficulties, respond to a counterargument and justify a conclusion.
technology.reading: Use this original text: ‘Access to a device can remove one barrier to homework, but access is not the same as effective learning. Pupils may also need a reliable connection, clear instructions and help when software fails. A lending scheme should therefore be evaluated using more than the number of devices borrowed. Schools could compare task completion, pupil feedback and requests for technical support. This evidence would show whether the scheme is convenient and whether it actually improves participation.’ Ask for the main argument, two barriers, the meaning of “evaluated”, an inference about borrowing figures and how the last sentence develops the argument.
technology.writing: Write an evaluation for a senior teacher deciding whether to introduce device lending. Present benefits, limitations, evidence the school should collect and a justified recommendation. Suggested length: 120–180 words for KS3; 180–250 for KS4/Post-16.

environment.name: Task set C — Local environment
environment.listening: Read aloud at a natural pace: ‘A student group measured lunchtime waste for five days. Disposable packaging filled most bins, while unopened food was the heaviest type of waste. The group recommended clearer recycling signs, a place for sharing sealed food and a meeting with catering staff about portion sizes. They will repeat the measurement next month to see which change has made a difference.’ Ask for the finding, two proposals, why measurement will be repeated and which proposal addresses food waste most directly.
environment.speaking: The pupil presents one realistic way to reduce school waste. Ask them to explain cause and effect, compare two possible actions, answer a challenge and justify how success should be measured.
environment.reading: Use this original text: ‘Waste data can make a problem visible, but figures need careful interpretation. A full bin may show that pupils are wasting more, or simply that collection happened later than usual. Repeated measurements taken in similar conditions are more reliable. Schools should also separate different kinds of waste because each may require a different response. Packaging can be reduced through purchasing decisions, whereas uneaten food may be linked to portion size, choice or lunchtime routines.’ Ask about the purpose, explicit comparison, “interpretation”, why conditions matter and how the final examples support the argument.
environment.writing: Write a proposal for reducing one kind of school waste. Use evidence, explain cause and effect, consider a limitation and describe how impact should be reviewed. Suggested length: 120–180 words for KS3; 180–250 for KS4/Post-16.

strategies.name: Slow breathing
strategies.instruction: Breathe in comfortably, pause briefly, then breathe out a little more slowly. Repeat without forcing the breath.

strategies.name: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
strategies.instruction: Notice five things you can see, four you can feel, three you can hear, two you can smell and one you can taste or imagine tasting.

strategies.name: Movement reset
strategies.instruction: Use a short walk, stretch, wall push or other agreed movement, then return to one clear next task.

strategies.name: Lower sensory load
strategies.instruction: Reduce noise, visual distraction or social demand where possible while keeping a clear route back to learning.

strategies.name: Water and reset
strategies.instruction: Use a brief drink or pause, then identify the smallest useful next step.

strategies.name: Break the task down
strategies.instruction: Write the next one to three steps only. Hide or ignore later steps until the first is complete.

strategies.name: Ask for help
strategies.instruction: Use the agreed help signal or sentence starter: “I understand ____. I am stuck on ____.”

strategies.name: Private rehearsal
strategies.instruction: Practise once privately or with a trusted partner before deciding whether to share more publicly.

strategies.name: Organise the workspace
strategies.instruction: Put away anything not needed, place the first resource ready and identify a clear start point.

strategies.name: Helpful self-talk
strategies.instruction: Use a realistic phrase such as “I can do the first step” or “Nerves can be here while I start.”

strategies.name: Co-regulate with an adult
strategies.instruction: Use a trusted adult, fewer words and a calmer space. Safety and safeguarding procedures take priority when required.

strategies.name: Short focus block
strategies.instruction: Choose one defined outcome, work until the timer ends, then review rather than committing to the whole task at once.

activities.name: 30-second state scan
activities.steps: Feet supported if possible. Notice energy, body tension and attention. Name what would help next.

activities.name: Box breathing visual
activities.steps: Trace a square slowly: breathe in, pause, breathe out, pause. Keep it comfortable rather than forcing a count.

activities.name: Desk stretch sequence
activities.steps: Stand, reach, shoulder roll, gentle twist, then sit and begin one clear starter item.

activities.name: One-step launch
activities.steps: Teacher or student identifies only the first action. Complete it before revealing or thinking about the next stage.

activities.name: Quiet reset
activities.steps: Move to the agreed lower-stimulation option, use minimal language and choose a clear return point.

activities.name: Worked-example restart
activities.steps: Compare current work with one modelled example, identify the next matching step, then retry independently.

activities.name: Partner rehearsal
activities.steps: Say or perform the response once privately. Partner gives one specific supportive improvement, then rehearse again.

activities.name: Transition countdown
activities.steps: Give a visible countdown, state exactly what ends and what begins, then acknowledge readiness rather than speed.

activities.name: Five-object grounding
activities.steps: Find five objects or visual details in the room and describe one neutral feature of each.

activities.name: Mini plan card
activities.steps: Write: 1) first task, 2) help route, 3) finish point. Cross off each as completed.

activities.name: Movement delivery job
activities.steps: Use a purposeful classroom movement task such as distributing resources, then return to a defined seat/task.

activities.name: End-of-lesson strategy review
activities.steps: What state did I notice? What did I try? Did it help a lot, a little or not yet? What will I repeat or change?

languageCoach.use: I can see this is a lot right now. Would fewer words, a quieter space, or help with the first step be useful?
languageCoach.why: Names the need without judging the feeling and offers manageable choices.

languageCoach.situation: Student is restless during independent work
languageCoach.use: It looks hard to keep your attention on this. Would a short movement reset or a five-minute focus block help?
languageCoach.why: Keeps the learning goal while offering a route to regulate.

languageCoach.avoid: You are choosing not to work.
languageCoach.use: Show me the last bit that made sense. We can choose the next one step from there.
languageCoach.why: Reduces task size and tests whether cognitive overload is part of the problem.

languageCoach.situation: Student is very excited in a practical
languageCoach.avoid: You need to be in Green.
languageCoach.use: The excitement is fine; we need enough control to hear the safety instruction. Equipment down, listen, then we restart.
languageCoach.why: Separates the emotional state from the safety requirement.

languageCoach.avoid: There is nothing to worry about.
languageCoach.use: Nerves can be here while you practise. Rehearse with one person first, then we will decide the next step.
languageCoach.why: Validates the state and preserves progression toward the learning goal.

languageCoach.use: Your energy looks low. Do you need water, a short movement reset, or help choosing the first small task?
languageCoach.why: Offers activation and structure without moralising low energy.

Start the next lesson with a predictable entry task

Plan sensory recovery after a busy space

Plan the move back to classroom learning

voiceQuestions: I know how to ask for a short regulation break without feeling embarrassed.
Adults usually use calm and respectful language when I am finding things difficult.
The strategies available in school actually help me return to learning.
Different teachers use similar language about regulation.
I know what to do if a strategy is not helping.
I can use regulation support without being treated as if I have done something wrong.
observationItems: Lesson structure and transitions are visible or clearly explained.
Staff language is descriptive and non-judgemental.
Students have a discreet route to ask for help or a reset.
Regulation support preserves access to the learning goal where possible.
Practical/group tasks use clear roles and checkpoints.
Reasonable sensory or communication supports are respected.
The close of the lesson supports a calm transition onward.
No zone is treated as a reward, sanction or behaviour label.
environmentCriteria: Noise load is understood and manageable
Visual clutter and competing displays are controlled
Entry, movement and exit routines are predictable
Students can ask for help discreetly
Movement/reset options are available where appropriate
Sensory needs can be supported without unnecessary attention
Seating/layout offers appropriate choice and clear sightlines
Key routines and expectations are easy to find

classroom: Keep the first task visible before students enter
Keep regulation tools easy to access without public attention
science: Separate safety instructions from background talk
ict: Provide a non-device fallback for login/device failure
art: Use process goals rather than comparison displays
music: Create quiet preparation space where possible
pe: Mark equipment and waiting zones clearly
corridor: Identify supervised reset points where appropriate

assessmentRoutines.name: 60-second grounding
steps: Look at the first instruction only

tripChecks: Food/medical arrangements checked through normal school procedures

safeguardingCategories.name: Everyday regulation / learning support
safeguardingCategories.message: Continue with the regulation workflow and normal classroom/pastoral support.

safeguardingCategories.name: Welfare concern needing adult follow-up
safeguardingCategories.message: Record and follow up using the school’s normal pastoral procedure. Do not rely on this app as the case-management record.

safeguardingCategories.name: Possible safeguarding concern
safeguardingCategories.message: Stop the regulation workflow and use the school’s safeguarding procedure immediately, including the DSL/appropriate safeguarding lead.

safeguardingCategories.name: Immediate safety or medical concern
safeguardingCategories.message: Use the school’s emergency/medical procedure now. This app is not an emergency-response system.

templates.body: Pre-check-in → first-step routine → agreed support route → post-assessment reflection

templates.name: Practical lesson regulation plan
templates.body: Preview equipment → allocate roles → pause at checkpoints → calm clean-down

templates.name: Difficult transition plan
templates.body: Preview → first step → support person → reset option → review

templates.name: Family review structure
templates.body: What is working → useful strategies → contexts needing support → agreed next step → review date
